items.title: TikTok Has Removed Hundreds of Thousands of Kenyan Videos. What Is Happening to Content on the Platform?
items.summary: TikTok removed 750,185 videos in Kenya between April and June 2026 (down 15% from Q1) for violating Community Guidelines, with 99.8% caught before user reports and 93.8% taken down within 24 hours. It also interrupted 80,640 Live sessions and removed over 46,000 suspected under-13 accounts.
items.content_html:
TikTok removed 750,185 videos in Kenya between April and June 2026 (down 15% from Q1) for violating Community Guidelines, with 99.8% caught before user reports and 93.8% taken down within 24 hours. It also interrupted 80,640 Live sessions and removed over 46,000 suspected under-13 accounts. About 11,000 videos fell under AI-generated/edited media policies. The report comes as Kenya considers stricter digital platform regulations.

Between April and June 2026, TikTok removed 750,185 videos in Kenya for violating its Community Guidelines, according to its latest enforcement report, released on November 9. These figures highlight how the platform moderates content, protects younger users, and deals with materials that are deemed to be harmful, misleading, or inappropriate.

The removals do not mean that every affected creator deliberately broke the rules or that every deleted video was illegal. TikTok’s guidelines cover several issues such as
•    Scams
•    Harassment
•    Dangerous activities
•    Sexual exploitation
•    Misinformation.

That said, the scale of enforcement also raises questions about automated moderation, appeals, and whether systems understand local languages and context.

TikTok Removed 750,185 Kenyan Videos in the Second Quarter

TikTok’s Q2 2026 Community Guidelines Enforcement Report says that the videos were removed between April 1 and June 30. This figure was down from 884,591 removals in the first quarter - a decrease of about 15%.

Notably, TikTok said that 99.8% of the Kenyan videos were removed before users reported them. While at it, 93.8% were taken down within 24 hours of posting. Additionally, the report recorded 80,640 TikTok Live sessions interrupted in Kenya for violating community guidelines. As if that is not enough, more than 46000 accounts suspected to belong to children below the age of 13 years were also removed. After all,13 is TikTok’s minimum age for a standard account – although some features have higher age requirements.

For context purposes, TikTok did not publish a Kenyan breakdown showing how many videos were removed under each policy. The platform did not also disclose the total number of videos uploaded in the country during the quarter. Therefore, the removals alone cannot show how common harmful content is among all Kenyan posts.

AI-Generated Content and Automated Moderation Raise Questions

Approximately 11,000 videos in Kenya were removed under TikTok’s policies on edited media and AI-generated content during the quarter. Nevertheless, that does not mean that all those videos were entirely AI-generated. As a matter of fact, the figure covers content falling under the relevant policy.

For creators, TikTok requires them to label realistic AI-generated material – especially realistic images, audio, and video. If anything, the platform uses detection systems and content credentials technology to help identify synthetic or significantly altered media. With the introduction of an in-app AI Literacy Hub in Kenya, users can now recognize AI-generated content and understand responsible use.

Globally, TikTok removed about 188.3 million videos from more than 42.2 billion uploaded during the same quarter. Automated systems were able to detect 97.4% of global removals. That said, about 6.3 million videos were reinstated after successful appeals.


What the Figures Mean for Kenyan Creators and Users

Creators ought to review TikTok’s Community Guidelines, label realistic AI-generated material and appeal removals they honestly believe that they’re mistaken. Remember that repeated violations can lead to account restrictions or bans. For Live creators, they need to check the rules that govern broadcasts and monetization.

Users can help by reporting scams, harassment, exploitation and dangerous content instead of sharing it further. Parents should pay attention to age requirements, privacy settings and the content children encounter.

The report comes as Kenya considers stronger regulations for digital platforms - particularly regarding harmful content, online child protection, and the responsibilities of technology companies. Proposed amendments to communications laws and the draft Online Safety Bill 2026 have intensified discussions about how platforms such as TikTok should monitor content, address complaints and protect users.

items.title: Vodafone's Sh68 Billion Safaricom Buyout: How It Was Self-Funded
items.summary: TL;DR: Vodafone sold a 5% effective stake in Safaricom to its own subsidiary, Vodacom, for Sh68 billion. Because Vodafone controls Vodacom, the money effectively returned to Vodafone—meaning the parent company funded its own exit from that slice of the business. The Kenyan government, by contrast,…
items.content_html:
TL;DR: Vodafone sold a 5% effective stake in Safaricom to its own subsidiary, Vodacom, for Sh68 billion. Because Vodafone controls Vodacom, the money effectively returned to Vodafone—meaning the parent company funded its own exit from that slice of the business. The Kenyan government, by contrast, received genuine external cash of Sh204 billion for its 15% stake.

The recent restructuring of Safaricom's ownership has raised eyebrows for a simple reason: Vodafone essentially used its own money to fund the purchase of its additional stake in East Africa's most profitable company. At the heart of the transaction is a Sh68 billion payment that Vodafone received from its African subsidiary, Vodacom, for transferring a 5% effective interest in Safaricom. In plain terms, Vodafone sold a slice of Safaricom to Vodacom, and the Sh68 billion price tag flowed back to the parent company.

The Intra-Group Transaction Explained

To understand how this works, it helps to look at the broader deal. Vodacom agreed to acquire an additional 20% of Safaricom, lifting its total shareholding to 55%. The breakdown was as follows:

  • 15% from the Kenyan government at a cost of Sh204 billion
  • 5% from Vodafone for Sh68 billion

Since Vodafone is the ultimate parent of Vodacom, the Sh68 billion that Vodacom paid for the 5% stake effectively returned to Vodafone's own coffers. In other words, Vodafone did not need to bring in fresh external capital to exit that portion of its Safaricom holding; the money circulated within the group.

Why Vodafone's Sh68 Billion Never Left the Family

This internal arrangement is a classic example of corporate simplification. Before the deal, the ownership structure involved multiple layers: Vodafone held a direct stake in Vodafone Kenya Limited, which in turn held shares in Safaricom, while Vodacom owned the majority of Vodafone Kenya.

By buying out Vodafone's remaining 12.5% stake in Vodafone Kenya Limited—equivalent to that 5% effective interest in Safaricom—Vodacom gained 100% ownership of the Kenyan holding vehicle. The Sh68 billion was the price of cleaning up that structure, and it went straight to Vodafone.

The Kenyan Government's Sh204 Billion External Payout

The Kenyan government, by contrast, received genuinely external funds. Its Sh204 billion payment from Vodacom for the 15% stake represents real cash entering the state's accounts, which the Treasury indicated would go toward infrastructure development and sovereign wealth funds.

Vodafone's Sh68 billion, however, was an intra-group transfer. Vodafone was both the seller of the 5% interest and, through its control of Vodacom, the ultimate source of the funds used to buy it.

A Neat Accounting Manoeuvre or Sensible Housekeeping?

Critics might describe this as a neat accounting manoeuvre. Supporters would call it sensible corporate housekeeping. Either way, the outcome is that Vodafone and Vodacom now fully consolidate Safaricom, gaining controlling ownership of a business with over 38 million M-Pesa customers and a market capitalisation of roughly €7.7 billion.

Vodafone's CEO, Margherita Della Valle, framed the move as a growth opportunity in an attractive market, noting the long partnership since 2000 that produced M-Pesa.

What This Means for Safaricom's NSE Listing

For Safaricom itself, the ownership change means little on the surface. The company remains listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, with the following shareholding structure:

  • Vodacom: 55%
  • Kenyan government: 20%
  • Public investors: 25%

But beneath the surface, the deal reveals how large multinationals can rearrange their African assets with minimal external cash outflow. Vodafone did not need to find a buyer for its Safaricom slice; it simply directed its own subsidiary to buy it, using funds that ultimately belonged to the group anyway. The Sh68 billion never left the family.

items.title: The 30-Day Rule: What Kenya Power Left Out of Its Shock Bill Defense
items.summary: TL;DR: Kenya Power's "as required by law" defense omits Section 159(1) of the Energy Act, 2019: if a faulty meter is reported and not inspected within 30 days, the utility can only back-bill 30 days of estimated use — not years. Keep written proof of…
items.content_html:
TL;DR: Kenya Power's "as required by law" defense omits Section 159(1) of the Energy Act, 2019: if a faulty meter is reported and not inspected within 30 days, the utility can only back-bill 30 days of estimated use — not years. Keep written proof of your report and cite this section if needed.

On the 11th of  November 2026, angry customers protested outside Kenya Power offices located in Naivasha and Roysambu over bills they said made no sense.

Of note was a Roysambu customer who became the face of the protest. She said her normal bill was approximately 300 Kshs per month. But then, out of the blue she received a bill of about 200,000 Kshs. 

She went on to lament that she had reported a faulty meter about two years earlier but nothing was done. She was therefore livid at the cost she is expected to bear.

In a bid to defend itself, Kenya Power responded on the 12th of November, saying  the Roysambu meter had an “anomaly” and that back-billing was done using the new meter’s average, “as required by law.”

But that phrase,  “as required by law”  is where the story gets complicated. Kenya Power didn't quote the law that actually protects customers who find themselves in this exact situation.

What’s the 30-day rule?

Section 159(1) of the Energy Act, 2019 states:

If a customer reports a faulty meter, The Kenya Power and Lighting Company must inspect it within 30 days.

If it fails to do so within the stipulated period, it is not allowed to come back later and charge for months or  years of estimated use. It can only recover 30 days of estimated consumption.

That is the limit. Thirty days. Not two years. Not 200,000 Kshs.

The law is designed for exactly this problem: a customer reports a fault, the utility delays, and the bill keeps increasing in the dark. In such a case, the customer should not be required to pay for the utility’s negligence.
What does this mean for the Roysambu customer?

If her claim is true and she reported the faulty meter two years ago,  then under Section 159(1), Kenya Power should only be able to recover 30 days of estimated consumption from her, not a two-year back-bill.

At her normal usage of about 300 Kshs a month, 30 days would be roughly 300 Kshs. Not 200,000 Kshs. That does not mean she owes nothing. Instead, it means what she owes is limited by law.

Kenya Power’s defense

Kenya Power is not wrong in stating that the law allows back-billing over faulty meters and using a new meter’s average to estimate past use is indeed a standard practice.

But by citing “the law” without mentioning Section 159(1), the company left out the part of the law that limits its own power.

Kenya Power argues the law justifies its shock bills but the law it is not quoting caps those bills at 30 days.

For customers, the lesson is simple: report a faulty meter in writing, be sure to keep proof of the date, and if 30 days pass without inspection, quote Section 159(1) in your defense.

items.title: Infinix Hot 60i Review: The NFC Budget Phone That Actually Makes Sense
items.summary: NFC is one of those features that budget phones usually skip. It is expensive to licence, rarely advertised in this price bracket, and most buyers do not know they want it until they try to use it. The Infinix Hot 60i includes it anyway, and…
items.content_html:
NFC is one of those features that budget phones usually skip. It is expensive to licence, rarely advertised in this price bracket, and most buyers do not know they want it until they try to use it. The Infinix Hot 60i includes it anyway, and in Kenya in 2026, that decision looks smarter than Infinix probably intended.

Safaricom and Pesapal have been rolling out Tap-to-Pay across merchant outlets in Kenya, allowing customers with NFC-enabled phones to tap on a POS terminal and complete an M-Pesa payment without entering a Till number . This is not a future concept. It is live at Java House, Artcaffé, and thousands of other retail outlets already using Pesapal terminals . A budget phone with NFC is no longer a novelty. It is a practical advantage.

But NFC alone does not make a phone worth buying. The Hot 60i has real strengths and real compromises. Here is what you actually get.

What the KES 14,899 Configuration Offers

The Hot 60i is sold in several configurations in Kenya, and the pricing is inconsistent. Jumia lists a 6GB/128GB model at KES 14,899 , while another listing shows an 8GB/256GB variant at KES 19,750 . A separate seller lists a 6GB/128GB unit at KES 23,500, which is clearly overpriced for this bracket . For the sub-15K buyer, the Jumia 6GB/128GB listing is the relevant model.

The processor is a MediaTek Helio G81 Ultimate, paired with Android 15 and Infinix's XOS 15.1 skin . The battery is 5,160mAh, and some listings claim 45W fast charging, though this figure varies by region and seller . The display is a 6.7-inch panel, and here the listings disagree sharply. Some sources list it as 720p , while one Jumia listing claims 1080x2460 FHD+ . You should confirm the resolution with the seller before paying, because the difference is significant.

The camera setup is a 50MP main sensor paired with a 2MP secondary lens, and an 8MP selfie camera . There is a side-mounted fingerprint sensor, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and stereo speakers . The microSD situation is also unclear across listings, so verify expandability if you need it.

The NFC Advantage in Kenya

This is the headline feature, and it deserves proper context.

M-Pesa Tap-to-Pay works by tapping an NFC-enabled phone on an NFC-enabled POS terminal, verifying the transaction details, and entering your M-Pesa PIN . It reduces queues, cuts down on wrong Till number entries, and speeds up checkout. For a Kenyan buyer who frequents supermarkets, coffee shops, or any merchant with a Pesapal terminal, this is a genuinely useful feature that most sub-15K phones do not offer.

The catch is that Tap-to-Pay is not universal yet. It works only at merchants with enabled POS devices, and the rollout is expanding but not complete . If you shop mostly at informal traders, kiosks, or matatu stages, you will not use NFC often. But if you live in Nairobi and pay at established retailers, the convenience is real.

The Compromises You Will Feel

The display is the biggest concern. If the Kenyan units are indeed 720p, text and images will look soft on a 6.7-inch screen. This is the standard trade-off in this bracket, but it is worth confirming before purchase because the listing information is contradictory.

The second compromise is storage speed. The Hot 60i uses eMMC 5.1 storage, which is slower than the UFS technology found in slightly more expensive phones . App launches and file transfers will feel slower than they should, especially if you are used to a faster device.

The third compromise is performance. The Helio G81 Ultimate is an entry-level chip. Benchmark results show a 3DMark Wild Life score of 648, with graphics tests running at roughly 4 frames per second . WhatsApp, M-Pesa, and browsing will work. Gaming and heavy multitasking will not. This is a phone for the basics.

The Verdict

Buy the Infinix Hot 60i if: you want NFC for M-Pesa Tap-to-Pay at a budget price, you need a large screen and a reliable battery for daily use, and you accept that this is a device for communication and light browsing rather than performance. The 6GB/128GB model at KES 14,899 is the version to target.

Skip it if: you can stretch to the Samsung Galaxy A07 for its six-year update promise, you need a confirmed sharp display and cannot verify the resolution before buying, or you rarely shop at merchants with NFC terminals. In those cases, the NFC advantage disappears, and the Hot 60i becomes an ordinary budget phone with an uncertain spec sheet.

The Infinix Hot 60i is not the best phone under KES 15,000 on raw performance. But it is the only one that anticipates how Kenyans will pay for things in the next few years. That makes it worth considering, provided you confirm exactly what you are buying.

Quick Verdict Card

Buy it if Skip it if
You want NFC for M-Pesa Tap-to-Pay at a budget price You cannot confirm the display resolution before buying
You need 6GB RAM and 128GB storage under KES 15,000 You want guaranteed long-term software updates (Samsung wins)
You shop regularly at Pesapal-enabled retailers You mostly buy from informal traders without NFC terminals

Value Score: 3 / 5 — The NFC feature is genuinely useful for urban Kenyan buyers, but the inconsistent spec listings and slow storage keep it from a higher score.

items.title: The Real Cost of "Cheap" Data: How Safaricom's B-Live Changes Are Hurting Small Buyers
items.summary: Samuel Waititu posted a complaint on Safaricom's social feed on 10 August 2026. The one-hour bundle was gone. B-Live was unavailable. Safaricom replied the same day that it was sorry and had taken his feedback. It did not say whether the product had been withdrawn,…
items.content_html:
Samuel Waititu posted a complaint on Safaricom's social feed on 10 August 2026. The one-hour bundle was gone. B-Live was unavailable. Safaricom replied the same day that it was sorry and had taken his feedback. It did not say whether the product had been withdrawn, restricted, or repriced .

The silence was the answer. Within days, Safaricom confirmed the new reality. Only one B-Live offering would remain: KES 25, available daily between 23:00 and 16:00 . The hours between 16:00 and 23:00, the exact window when a boda rider finishes a shift, a student opens a laptop, and a trader posts stock to WhatsApp Status, were no longer covered.

No price was raised. The shilling figure on the menu did not change. But the product that made data affordable for millions of Kenyans was quietly removed, and the effective cost of getting online for an afternoon rose by half.

What B-Live Was, and What It Became

B-Live was built for people who could not pre-commit KES 1,000 for a monthly bundle. It sold time instead of volume. KES 20 bought an hour. KES 50 bought three hours. KES 150 bought six . For a trader with KES 50 in M-Pesa and an uncertain day ahead, that was the only way to get online at all.

The new structure is different. The KES 20 hourly option is gone. What remains is KES 25 for one hour, plus ten voice minutes, available only outside the evening peak . The hourly price rose 25 per cent. The multi-hour blocks that let someone plan an afternoon online disappeared. The effective cost of that afternoon rose from KES 16.67 an hour to KES 25, an increase of 50 per cent .

And the seven hours between 16:00 and 23:00? No B-Live access at all.

Who This Hurts, and Why the Numbers Prove It

The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics recorded 18.1 million people in informal employment in 2025, against 3.31 million in formal wage employment. That is 83.8 per cent of all jobs . These workers are paid when a fare is completed or a harvest sells. They do not have a salary date. They cannot pre-commit KES 1,000 for thirty days, no matter how good the per-gigabyte price looks on paper.

The Communications Authority estimates average data use at about 5GB a month per subscription. Safaricom's own audited figure is 4.92GB. But the average hides a split. Roughly half of Safaricom's mobile data subscribers use less than 1GB in a month . For that half, the hourly bundle was not a marginal product. It was the entire product. Safaricom's chief financial officer described these customers as a "large opportunity" .

Removing the product they rely on is not a pricing adjustment. It is removing the entry point.

The Other Side of the Same Campaign

In the same three weeks that B-Live was gutted, Safaricom launched Pata More. The KES 1,000 monthly bundle went from 10GB to 21.5GB. The implied cost per gigabyte fell from KES 100 to roughly KES 47 . The KES 20 daily bundle rose from 150MB to 250MB. The KES 99 bundle rose from 1GB to 1.5GB .

These are real improvements. For anyone who buys monthly, Safaricom is cheaper than it was before. But the campaign was not designed for the buyer who survives on KES 20 at a time. It was designed for the buyer who can pay KES 1,000 upfront. Safaricom protected its high-value customers while stripping value from its smallest ones.

Airtel made its own adjustments. Its KES 1,000 bundle now gives 25GB, still more than Safaricom's 21.5GB . But the gap has narrowed dramatically. Before these changes, Airtel's advantage at the monthly tier was enormous. The KES 1,500 Smarta bundle once gave 90GB. It now gives 32GB . Airtel did not cut prices to compete. It cut value while keeping the price the same, then watched Safaricom do the same to its small buyers.

What Safaricom Has Not Said

Safaricom has described the B-Live changes as a review of data bundles. A congestion rationale is plausible. On 1 August, the company announced 300 additional masts, which is what a congestion constraint would call for . But Safaricom has not made that argument publicly. It has not explained why the evening hours, the busiest and most valuable window, were the ones removed. It has not said whether the decision will be reversed.

The company's financial position does not make the case easier to accept. Safaricom's Kenyan EBITDA margin reached 56.8 per cent in the year to March 2026, while capital expenditure fell 18.4 per cent. The declared dividend rose 66.7 per cent to KES 80 billion. Data revenue of KES 83.4 billion overtook voice for the first time . A company with expanding margins and falling capital intensity is not forced to remove the cheapest way its poorest customers get online.

The Verdict

If you buy monthly: you are better off than you were last year. The KES 1,000 bundle gives more than double the data it did before. Stay with Safaricom if coverage matters. Switch to Airtel if you want 25GB instead of 21.5GB at the same price.

If you buy daily or hourly: you have been hit hardest. The B-Live product you relied on is gone. The replacement covers hours you do not need and excludes the hours you do. Your options are to buy volume-based daily bundles that cost more per megabyte, or to stretch to a weekly or monthly bundle you may not be able to afford.

The truth nobody says out loud: Safaricom did not raise the price of cheap data. It removed the definition of cheap data that millions of Kenyans depended on. The price tag stayed the same. The door closed anyway.

Quick Verdict Card

If you buy monthly If you buy daily or hourly
You are better off: KES 1,000 now gives 21.5GB You are worse off: the hourly B-Live options are gone
Stay with Safaricom for coverage, or Airtel for 25GB The KES 25 replacement excludes 16:00–23:00
The per-GB cost has fallen to roughly KES 47 Your effective hourly cost rose from KES 16.67 to KES 25

Value Score: 2 / 5 for small buyers — The monthly tier improved, but the removal of affordable hourly access is a direct cost to the Kenyans who can least absorb it.
